lessons.title: le père, la mère — the oldest words in the family
lessons.gloss: father and mother — the PIE root behind paternal and maternal

segments.text: The words for "father" and "mother" are among the oldest words we can reconstruct — older than Latin, older than Rome. French kept them almost bare: père and mère. And they are secretly the same words as English father and mother.
le père ("father") from Latin pater from PIE ph₂tḗr.
la mère ("mother") from Latin māter from PIE méh₂tēr.
Note the articles: le père (masculine), la mère (feminine) — the gender you have been tracking since Chapter 1.
French took pater/māter straight from Latin. English took the same PIE words down a different road, through Grimm's law, which turned Latin's p becomes f and t becomes th:

utterances: PIE: ph₂tḗr. Latin / French: pater becomes père. English: father.
PIE: méh₂tēr. Latin / French: māter becomes mère. English: mother.

segments.text: So père and father are not lookalikes borrowed late — they are the same inherited word, one keeping the p, the other shifting it to f. The Latin root also gives English its "of a parent" adjectives: paternal, paternity, patron and maternal, maternity, matron, matter (māter becomes materia, "stuff a tree-mother makes").

segments.text: Give "father" and "mother" with their articles. (le père, la mère.) What one sound-change makes père into English father? (Grimm's law: p becomes f — and t becomes th.) Name an English cousin of each. (père becomes paternal/patron; mère becomes maternal/matron.) Next: le frère, la sœur — brother and sister.

lessons.title: le frère, la sœur — brother and sister
lessons.gloss: brother and sister — frater and soror, behind fraternal and sorority

segments.text: With parents in hand, the next pair: frère ("brother") and sœur ("sister"). Both are straight from Latin, and both hand English a whole family of words.
le frère ("brother") from Latin frāter from PIE bʰréh₂tēr (the same PIE root that, through Grimm's law bʰ becomes b, gave English brother).
la sœur ("sister") from Latin soror. The odd-looking œ (an o and e fused into one letter) spells the vowel that soror wore down to — soror becomes seror becomes sœur.
frère becomes fraternal, fraternity, fraternize, and — softened in old French — friar (a "brother" in a religious order).

sœur becomes sorority, sororal; and a sister in a convent is still called a sœur. (English sister comes from the same PIE root swésōr, by the Germanic road — Latin soror and English sister are cousins.)
So the four family words now form a set: père, mère, frère, sœur — each one a key to a Latin-through-English word (paternal, maternal, fraternal, sorority).
